Simulating the effect of missed or delayed samples around Tmax on NCA parameters

Jerry Hu

2026-09-21

← PK/PD Home Page

1 Summary

Background. Real blood-sampling schedules deviate from plan. A sample near the peak can be missed, or drawn later than planned. The objective is to quantify how much a single missed or delayed sample around Tmax biases the key NCA exposure parameters (Cmax, AUC0-t, AUC0-inf) relative to a planned schedule.

Methods. Simulation, NCA, tables and figures, and the statistical analysis were all conducted in R. Concentration–time data were simulated from three one-compartment oral pharmacokinetic models with differing absorption and elimination rates, from 0 to 24 h after a single oral dose (20 subjects per model). The typical time of peak was held at about 0.5 h, so the three profiles differ mainly in peak shape, from a flat plateau to a sharp peak; between-subject variability moves each subject’s own peak time around that. Three sampling schedules were applied to the same subjects: a planned 13-sample schedule, an omission schedule with the near-peak sample dropped, and a delay schedule with that sample drawn 10 minutes late. NCA derived Cmax, AUC0-t and AUC0-inf from each schedule. Each deviating schedule was then compared with the planned schedule in the same subjects, as a paired geometric mean ratio with a 90% confidence interval on the log scale, and the spread of the individual ratios was summarised. The planned schedule was also compared with each subject’s true value — the same NCA applied to their noise-free predicted profile.

Results. A missed near-peak sample lowered Cmax by 2.6-7.7% across shapes (most in the sharply peaked profile), while it lowered AUC0-t by 0.1-2.5% and AUC0-inf by 0.2-2.5%. A delayed sample, analysed at its actual draw time, changed Cmax by −4.2% to +1.6% and both AUCs by −1.5% to +0.1%. Individual subjects deviated more than the mean: the lowest single-subject Cmax ratio after a missed sample was 74.7% of planned. The planned schedule itself overstated Cmax by 4.3-4.9% relative to the true value, on assay noise alone. Across both deviations the largest change was in Cmax; a single missed or delayed near-peak sample moved NCA exposure only slightly on average.

2 Background

Blood-sampling schedules in clinical pharmacokinetics are finite and planned in advance. The non-compartmental (NCA) parameters they yield — Cmax, Tmax, and the areas under the curve (AUC) — feed exposure and labelling decisions. Unplanned deviations disturb those schedules: a sample is missed, or a sample is drawn late. Sampling near the peak matters most for Cmax and Tmax, because those two estimates depend on whether the measurements capture the maximum at all; the sharper the peak, the more sensitive they are to a gap around it.

Objective. Quantify how much a single missed or delayed sample around Tmax biases the key NCA exposure parameters (Cmax, AUC0-t, AUC0-inf) relative to a planned schedule.

3 Methods

3.1 Simulation

3.1.1 Simulation model

The data were simulated with the R package mrgsolve. The structural model is one compartment with first-order oral absorption: a dosing compartment (GUT) feeds a central compartment (CENT), parameterised by absorption rate ka, clearance CL, and volume V. The model is shown below:

One-compartment model with first-order oral absorption. Dose enters the GUT compartment, is absorbed into CENT at rate ka, and is cleared from CENT at rate CL/V.

\[ \frac{dA_{\mathrm{GUT}}}{dt} = -k_a\,A_{\mathrm{GUT}}, \qquad \frac{dA_{\mathrm{CENT}}}{dt} = k_a\,A_{\mathrm{GUT}} - \frac{CL}{V}\,A_{\mathrm{CENT}}, \qquad C = \frac{A_{\mathrm{CENT}}}{V}. \]

where \(A_{\mathrm{GUT}}\) is the amount of drug in the absorption (gut) compartment, \(A_{\mathrm{CENT}}\) the amount in the central compartment, \(k_a\) the first-order absorption rate constant, \(CL\) the clearance, \(V\) the central volume of distribution, and \(C\) the plasma concentration (\(C = A_{\mathrm{CENT}}/V\)).

The model is defined in mrgsolve. The $OMEGA and $SIGMA blocks carry the between-subject and residual variability described below:

# --- data-generating model -------------------------------------------
# OMEGA = log(1 + CV^2) for 30% log-normal CV ≈ 0.0862 (variance scale).
# SIGMA = (0.10)^2 = 0.01 for 10% proportional RUV (variance scale).
.model_code <- '
$PARAM
// Placeholders only: every run overrides these with the profile it simulates
// (see the typical parameters below).
TVKA = 5.2, TVCL = 25, TVV = 50

$CMT GUT CENT

$OMEGA @labels ETA_KA ETA_CL ETA_V
0.0862 0.0862 0.0862

$SIGMA @labels PROP
0.01

$PK
double KA = TVKA * exp(ETA_KA);
double CL = TVCL * exp(ETA_CL);
double V  = TVV  * exp(ETA_V);

$ODE
dxdt_GUT  = -KA * GUT;
dxdt_CENT =  KA * GUT - (CL/V) * CENT;

$ERROR
double IPRED = CENT / V;
double DV = IPRED * (1 + PROP);

$CAPTURE IPRED DV KA CL V
'

mod <- mrgsolve::mcode("oral_1cmt", .model_code, quiet = TRUE)

Between-subject variability is log-normal on ka, CL and V (30% coefficient of variation each). Residual error is proportional (10%).

3.1.2 Profile shapes

The three profiles share a typical peak of 1.5 mg/L at a typical peak time near 0.5 h, differing only in how fast the drug is eliminated relative to how fast it is absorbed. The common peak height is by construction: ka and kel set each profile’s shape, and V is then chosen to put all three peaks on the same concentration, with CL = kel × V preserving the elimination rate. The comparison is therefore one of peak shape rather than concentration scale, at the cost that V differs across the profiles. Both shared quantities are typical values, not fixed ones: between-subject variability gives individual true Cmax a range of 0.62-2.33 mg/L and individual true Tmax 0.32-0.92 h. The profiles are named for the shape of the resulting peak: for this model the curvature of the peak, relative to Cmax, is proportional to ka × kel, so the Plateau profile (ka × kel ≈ 0.9) rises fast and then barely declines, while the Peaked profile (ka × kel ≈ 3.6) has the sharpest peak.

The three profile shapes. The typical Tmax is near 0.5 h and the typical Cmax the same in all three, so the deviating sample lands in the same place each time and the profiles differ in peak shape rather than in concentration scale.
Profile ka (1/h) kel (1/h) CL (L/h) V (L) t1/2 (h) Tmax (h) Cmax (mg/L) Shape
Plateau 9.1 0.1 6.34 63.4 6.93 0.5 1.5 Fast rise to a flat plateau; slow decline
Moderate 5.2 0.5 25.98 52.0 1.39 0.5 1.5 Moderate peak and decline
Peaked 3.3 1.1 42.34 38.5 0.63 0.5 1.5 Sharp peak; fast decline

Each profile has 20 subjects. The three profiles share the same dose, sample size and sampling times, and are simulated at one-minute resolution, from which each sampling schedule is then selected:

# --- study design -----------------------------------------------
N_SUBJ        <- 20
DOSE_MG       <- 100
NOMINAL_TIMES <- c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24)
DELAY_TIME    <- 0.5 + 10/60                       # 10-min delay → 0.6667 h
MINUTE_GRID   <- seq(0, 24, by = 1/60)             # 1-min resolution

# --- typical parameters per profile -------------------------------
# Each profile's SHAPE is set by its (ka, kel) pair; all three give Tmax in
# [0.495, 0.505] h via ln(ka/kel)/(ka-kel). V is then chosen so every profile
# peaks at the same typical, noise-free concentration, and CL = kel * V keeps
# the elimination rate. Matching the peaks means the profiles differ in peak
# SHAPE and not in concentration scale, which is what the study compares; V
# therefore differs across profiles rather than being 50 L throughout.
TARGET_CMAX_MGL <- 1.5

tv_from_shape <- function(ka, kel, dose = DOSE_MG, cmax_target = TARGET_CMAX_MGL) {
  tmax <- log(ka / kel) / (ka - kel)
  v    <- (dose * ka) / (ka - kel) *
            (exp(-kel * tmax) - exp(-ka * tmax)) / cmax_target
  list(TVKA = ka, TVCL = kel * v, TVV = v)
}

profile_params <- list(
  plateau  = tv_from_shape(9.1, 0.1),
  moderate = tv_from_shape(5.2, 0.5),
  peaked   = tv_from_shape(3.3, 1.1)
)

# --- simulate -------------------------------------------------------
simulate_profile <- function(profile_name, pars) {
  mod_s <- param(mod, pars)
  events <- expand.ev(ID = seq_len(N_SUBJ), amt = DOSE_MG, cmt = 1)
  all_times <- sort(unique(c(MINUTE_GRID, NOMINAL_TIMES, DELAY_TIME)))

  sim <- mod_s |>
    data_set(events) |>
    mrgsim(end = 24, add = all_times, obsonly = TRUE) |>
    as.data.frame()

  # ODE solver can return tiny negatives at late times when true concentration
  # is ~machine epsilon (peaked profile, t > ~10 h). Set to zero.
  sim$IPRED <- pmax(sim$IPRED, 0)
  sim$DV    <- pmax(sim$DV,    0)
  sim$PROFILE <- profile_name
  sim
}

Plotted on a semi-log scale over the full 24 h, the three shapes differ only in how sharply they rise and fall. The y-axis is floored at 1 ng/mL, a plausible assay limit for this concentration range.

Simulated mean concentration-time profile for each profile shape (Plateau, Moderate, Peaked), semi-log, from the noise-free model predictions at one-minute resolution. The typical peak height and peak time are matched across the three, so the shapes differ in peak sharpness and decline. These are means over the 20 simulated subjects, so they sit a little above the matched typical peak and need not coincide exactly.

3.1.3 Sampling schedules

Three sampling schedules are applied to the same per-subject time-courses, so each subject acts as its own control across schedules:

The three sampling schedules. All three are selected from the same simulated time-courses, so every comparison is within-subject.
Schedule Samples (0-24 h) Sampling times (h) Purpose
Planned 13 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24 Reference schedule
Omission 12 Planned times with the 0.5 h sample dropped Missed near-Tmax sample
Delay 13 Planned times, but the 0.5 h sample drawn at 0.667 h (+10 min) Delayed near-Tmax sample

The planned 13-sample schedule is the reference. The omission and delay schedules each alter the single 0.5 h near-peak sample: omission drops it, and delay replaces it with the draw at 0.667 h:

# --- sampling schedules -----------------------------------------------------
planned <- profiles_sim |>
  filter(in_set(time, NOMINAL_TIMES)) |>
  transmute(PROFILE, ID, SCHEDULE = "planned",
            TIME_PLANNED = round(time, 6),
            TIME_ACTUAL  = round(time, 6),
            CONC = DV)

omission <- planned |>
  filter(!near(TIME_PLANNED, 0.5)) |>
  mutate(SCHEDULE = "omission")

delayed_sample <- profiles_sim |>
  filter(in_set(time, DELAY_TIME)) |>
  transmute(PROFILE, ID, SCHEDULE = "delay",
            TIME_PLANNED = 0.5,
            TIME_ACTUAL  = round(time, 6),
            CONC = DV)

delay <- bind_rows(
  planned |> filter(!near(TIME_PLANNED, 0.5)) |> mutate(SCHEDULE = "delay"),
  delayed_sample
) |> arrange(PROFILE, ID, TIME_ACTUAL)

obs <- bind_rows(planned, omission, delay)

3.2 NCA

NCA is performed with the R package PKNCA, over the 0–last and 0–inf intervals, using the linear-up / log-down trapezoidal rule for the AUC. The reported parameters are Cmax, AUC0-t and AUC0-inf (primary) and Tmax (secondary). AUC0-inf requires a terminal slope, so λz is estimated internally as a dependency; it is not reported, and terminal-phase parameters are out of scope. The same NCA settings are applied to every schedule, at the actual sample times:

# NCA interval: 0 to infinity. lambda.z is requested because aucinf.obs needs it.
NCA_INTERVAL <- data.frame(
  start      = 0,
  end        = Inf,
  cmax       = TRUE,
  tmax       = TRUE,
  auclast    = TRUE,
  aucinf.obs = TRUE,
  lambda.z   = TRUE
)

# Parameters reported: Cmax, Tmax, AUC0-t, AUC0-inf.
NCA_PARAMS_WIDE <- c("cmax", "tmax", "auclast", "aucinf.obs")

#' Run NCA on one sampling schedule across all (PROFILE, ID), at the actual sample times.
#'
#' @param obs       Long observation data (PROFILE, ID, SCHEDULE, TIME_*, CONC).
#' @param schedule  Schedule to subset ("planned", "omission", "delay").
#' @param run_label Label tagged onto the output (e.g. "PLANNED").
#' @return Long PKNCA result with RUN_LABEL attached.
run_nca_schedule <- function(obs, schedule, run_label) {
  stopifnot(schedule %in% unique(obs$SCHEDULE))

  sub <- obs %>%
    filter(SCHEDULE == schedule) %>%
    transmute(PROFILE, ID, TIME = TIME_ACTUAL, CONC) %>%
    arrange(PROFILE, ID, TIME)

  conc_obj <- PKNCAconc(sub, CONC ~ TIME | PROFILE + ID)
  dose_df <- sub %>% distinct(PROFILE, ID) %>% mutate(TIME = 0, DOSE = 1)
  dose_obj <- PKNCAdose(dose_df, DOSE ~ TIME | PROFILE + ID)

  pk_res <- pk.nca(PKNCAdata(conc_obj, dose_obj, intervals = NCA_INTERVAL))
  out <- as.data.frame(pk_res$result)
  out$RUN_LABEL <- run_label
  out
}

Each subject also has a true value for every parameter: the same NCA applied to that subject’s noise-free individual predictions (IPRED) at one-minute resolution. It is not a schedule anyone could run — it is what the schedules are measured against. Because a one-compartment oral model has closed forms for all four parameters, the true values are checked against them (Tmax = ln(ka/kel)/(ka − kel), AUC0-inf = dose/CL, and the corresponding expressions for Cmax and AUC0-24); they agree to within 0.03% on the exposures and half a minute on Tmax.

3.3 Statistical analysis

The analysis follows the SAP with documented amendments; changes made after results were available are identified in its dated amendment log. All comparisons are paired by subject.

For each of the three ratio parameters (Cmax, AUC0-t, AUC0-inf), the per-subject ratio of the deviating schedule to the planned schedule is computed on the log scale and summarised as the geometric mean ratio, GMR = exp(mean of the per-subject log-ratios). Each GMR is reported with a 90% confidence interval from the paired t-distribution on the log scale; 100% denotes no effect. The spread of the individual ratios is summarised as the geometric CV of the paired ratios (from the SD of the log-ratios), the 5th–95th percentiles, and the minimum and maximum. The planned schedule is compared with the true value on the same footing.

Tmax is summarised descriptively, as the distribution of recorded Tmax under each schedule, because it can only take one of the scheduled sampling times. The omission schedule has no 0.5 h sample, so the 25 of 60 profiles that peaked there under the planned schedule are forced elsewhere — some of the shift is the gap itself.

The estimator takes the per-subject log-ratios, averages them, and back-transforms the mean and its paired-t interval to the ratio scale:

#' GMR + 90% CI for the ratio parameters (paired log-scale estimator).
#' @return per (PROFILE, parameter, contrast): n, gmr, ci_lo, ci_hi.
gmr_summary <- function(pairs) {
  pairs %>%
    filter(parameter %in% PARAMS_RATIO,
           is.finite(theta_test), is.finite(theta_ref),
           theta_test > 0, theta_ref > 0) %>%
    group_by(PROFILE, parameter, contrast) %>%
    summarise(
      n            = n(),
      mean_logdiff = mean(log(theta_test) - log(theta_ref)),
      sd_logdiff   = sd(log(theta_test) - log(theta_ref)),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      se        = sd_logdiff / sqrt(n),
      tcrit     = qt(0.95, n - 1),          # 90% CI
      gmr       = exp(mean_logdiff),
      ci_lo     = exp(mean_logdiff - tcrit * se),
      ci_hi     = exp(mean_logdiff + tcrit * se)
    ) %>%
    select(profile = PROFILE, parameter, contrast,
           n, gmr, ci_lo, ci_hi)
}

4.2.2 Tmax (secondary)

Tmax by sampling schedule (Planned, Omission, Delay) and profile shape, with the true peak time alongside. Boxes span the interquartile range; a recorded Tmax can only take one of the scheduled sampling times.

Recorded Tmax is the time of the largest measured concentration. Omission changes it only when the removed 0.5 h sample was the recorded maximum; the new Tmax is then the time of the largest remaining measurement, which may be earlier or later and need not be adjacent. After delay, Tmax is the time of the largest measurement among the retained samples and the replacement draw — it may move earlier, later, or remain unchanged. Each panel shows where the peak was recorded under each schedule, not how far individual subjects moved. Dropping the 0.5 h sample moved the recorded Tmax for 5, 7 and 13 of 20 subjects in the Plateau, Moderate and Peaked profiles respectively — the rest peaked elsewhere already and were untouched.

4.3 Statistical analysis

4.3.1 Geometric mean ratios

Geometric mean ratio (test ÷ reference schedule) with 90% CI, by parameter, profile shape and comparison. 100% denotes no effect.

The forest plot and table report each geometric mean ratio with its 90% CI, by parameter and profile shape. A missed near-peak sample lowered Cmax by 2.6-7.7% across the three shapes (geometric mean ratio 92.32%-97.38%), most in the Peaked profile, and lowered AUC0-t by 0.1-2.5% and AUC0-inf by 0.2-2.5%. A delayed sample, analysed at its actual draw time, changed Cmax by −4.2% to +1.6% (geometric mean ratio 95.79%-101.59%) and both AUCs by −1.5% to +0.1%.

These ratios span several parameters and profile shapes and are read as ranges describing magnitude, not as multiplicity-controlled tests.

The third comparison asks a different question: what does a complete, well-placed schedule cost against the truth? The planned schedule brackets the peak by design — 0.5 h is a scheduled time — yet it still returned a Cmax 104.26%-104.92% of the true value, higher by 4.3-4.9%. Almost none of that is a missed peak, and what there is runs the other way: taking the same 13 samples from the noise-free curve gives 98.83%-99.66% of the true Cmax, so the sampling grid loses about 0.3-1.2%. The overshoot is the assay. Cmax is the largest of the measurements taken around the peak, and the largest of several noisy draws sits above the concentration they are measuring — by enough to more than cancel the grid’s loss. AUC is not subject to that maximum selection: a trapezoidal integral averages across the measurements rather than picking the largest. Planned AUC0-t was 97.68%-99.55% of truth and AUC0-inf 97.68%-100.45%. Those differences reflect the combined effects of sampling and residual error under the chosen NCA method, and AUC0-inf also depends on the estimated terminal slope.

For Cmax after a missed near-peak sample, the geometric CV of the paired ratios was 5.2-8.6% and the lowest single-subject ratio was 74.7% of planned (5th percentile 82.47%-89.22% across profile shapes). After a delayed sample the single-subject Cmax ratios ranged from 74.7% to 121.5% — the widest individual spread of any comparison, because a sample 10 min later can fall on either side of a noisy peak. The AUC ratios were far tighter: no individual AUC0-t or AUC0-inf ratio fell below 92.5% or above 102.7%.

4.4 Results Summary

The objective was to quantify how much a single missed or delayed sample around Tmax biases the key NCA exposure parameters (Cmax, AUC0-t, AUC0-inf) relative to a planned schedule. Across the three profile shapes:

Effect on Cmax.

  • Omission vs Planned: Cmax was 92.32%-97.38% of planned (lower by 2.6-7.7%) — the largest effect of either deviation, because dropping the near-peak sample widens the gap between the sampled maximum and the true peak; the sharper the peak, the larger the loss.
  • Delay vs Planned: Cmax was 95.79%-101.59% of planned (a change of −4.2% to +1.6%); the sample drawn 10 min late still lands near the peak, and on the Plateau profile can even exceed the 0.5 h value.
  • Individual subjects: the single-subject Cmax ratio fell as low as 74.7% after a missed sample, and ranged from 74.7% to 121.5% after a delayed one.
  • Against the truth: even with every sample collected on time, Cmax came out 4.3-4.9% above the true value.

Effect on AUC (AUC0-t and AUC0-inf).

  • Omission lowered AUC0-t by 0.1-2.5% and AUC0-inf by 0.2-2.5%; delay moved both by −1.5% to +0.1%. The largest absolute change in any of those geometric mean ratios was 2.5% (Peaked profile, omission). No individual subject’s AUC ratio fell outside 92.5%–102.7%; one near-peak point is a small part of the exposure integral.

Effect on Tmax.

  • Omission moved the recorded Tmax to another scheduled time for 5, 7 and 13 of 20 subjects (Plateau, Moderate, Peaked) — those whose peak had been recorded at the missing 0.5 h sample. The replacement was not always the neighbouring time, and was sometimes earlier. Delay recorded Tmax at the +10 min draw whenever that sample was the largest measurement.

5 Discussion

We simulated single-dose concentration–time data from three one-compartment oral PK models spanning slow to fast elimination — and, as a result, a flat plateau to a sharp peak — applied three sampling schedules to the same subjects, derived the NCA parameters from each, and compared each deviating schedule with the planned schedule as a paired geometric mean ratio with a 90% confidence interval.

  • Cmax. A missed near-peak sample produced the largest change, lowering Cmax by 2.6-7.7% on average; a sample drawn 10 min late changed it by −4.2% to +1.6%. The loss grows with peak sharpness, so it is the Peaked (fast-elimination) profile that is most exposed. These ratios are relative to the planned practical schedule, and they assume the deviation falls on the near-Tmax sample; a deviation elsewhere on the curve would affect Cmax less. The delay result also assumes the actual draw time is recorded and used in the analysis; a delayed sample analysed at its planned time would behave differently and was not studied here.
  • Individual subjects. The mean effect understates what can happen to one subject: the lowest single-subject Cmax ratio after a missed sample was 74.7% of planned. For a study-level GMR a single deviating subject contributes only its share of the mean, but for a single-subject data query or an outlier assessment the individual ratio is the relevant quantity.
  • AUC. The largest absolute change in any AUC0-t or AUC0-inf geometric mean ratio under either deviation was 2.5% (Peaked profile, omission), because a single near-peak point is a small fraction of the integral. These results do not establish the effects of deviations at other times or of multiple missing samples.
  • Tmax. Omission shifts the recorded Tmax to whichever remaining sample is largest, and delay can shift it to the later draw, so Tmax tracks the sampling times directly rather than the underlying peak. It also ran later than the real peak time with no deviation at all: on the Plateau profile the median true Tmax is 0.47 h, but the planned schedule recorded 0.75 h. Two things are consistent with that — the schedule can only report a time it sampled, and on a flat, slowly-declining peak many time points sit within assay noise of the maximum, so the largest measurement can land on any of them. This study did not separate the two contributions. Observed Tmax should therefore be read as approximate.
  • A complete schedule still overstates Cmax. Compared with each subject’s true value, the planned schedule returned a Cmax higher by 4.3-4.9%, even though 0.5 h is a scheduled sample and the peak is bracketed by design. Two effects run against each other and the assay wins: sampling at 13 points rather than continuously loses 0.3-1.2% of the peak, while Cmax being a maximum over noisy measurements adds more than that back. The upward component grows with the number of samples near the peak — the opposite direction to the loss from a missed sample, and a reason to read an absolute Cmax more cautiously than a within-study Cmax ratio. AUC is not subject to maximum selection: AUC0-t came out 97.68%-99.55% of truth and AUC0-inf 97.68%-100.45%.

Other limitations.

  • A single delay magnitude (+10 min on the 0.5 h sample), a single missed sample, and 20 subjects per profile were studied. Larger delays, multiple deviations, deviations at later time points, and a coarser schedule around the peak (the planned schedule samples every 15 min from 0.25 to 1 h, denser than many Phase 1 designs) would give different numbers.
  • No lower limit of quantification was applied, and sensitivity to BLQ handling was not evaluated. Applying an LLOQ could move the last quantifiable sample earlier, changing AUC0-t and potentially the terminal fit and the AUC0-inf extrapolation. The small extrapolated tail under the current analysis does not establish insensitivity to those changes. Terminal parameters are estimated internally as needed for AUC0-inf but are not reported as study endpoints.
  • The reference for the primary comparisons is the planned practical schedule, so those ratios are “deviating vs planned schedule”. The separate comparison against each subject’s true value is what places the planned schedule itself.
